rv.q: Les Waters's staging of this play — Smith's Off Broadway debut — for Atlantic Theater Company is marvelously realized, as much, at least, as Smith's often maddening script allows.
Grief Camp offers a strikingly unsentimental and thoughtful panorama of young people who refuse to let grief hold them back from living.
Grief Camp, a haunting, humane new play by the 27-year-old (!) Eliya Smith, premiering in an excellent Atlantic Theater production.
I felt glad to be in the presence of such a thoughtful and free-spirited writer, who, in taking great care with her characters' feelings, respects ours.
But there's a line between realism and dullness, and Grief Camp straddles that border.
Even the play’s brief 100-minute runtime can’t prevent the onset of ennui, not unlike what the restless kids on display might feel when the weather remains too damp or hot to have any fun.
Grief Camp does nothing fruitful with the concept, providing aimless quirkiness instead of the emotion that might make us feel anything but boredom.
Unfortunately, that ends up turning Grief Camp into an Annie Baker-style writing exercise, where the playwright discovers that she's not Annie Baker.
In the end, the experience of watching Grief Camp might mirror the experience of grief itself: confusing, directionless, unresolvable—but ultimately, strangely freeing.
Grief Camp creates a vivid, fully inhabited world and assembles conditions ripe for drama, but never shapes them into a story.

But there’s also a diffuseness here, with interactions that lead to nowhere in terms of character development or building the narrative, and moments of theatricality like onstage rain (effects by Jeremy Chernick) that lead to neither confrontation nor catharsis.
This is one of the strongest shows of the off-Broadway season.

Smith and Tony-nominated director Les Waters (Dana H., Big Love) carefully avoid any lapses into sentimentality or solipsism, treating Cade and the campers like unique characters in their own right and not as plot points to rhapsodize about grief.

vr.q: I think by the end, it has given you plenty to chew on and is very satisfying in that sense.
